title: Scientific thinking
folderRuns: Scientific thinking, Circuits, Science puzzles, Quantum computing
blurb: Puzzles about the physical world, and how to reason your way through them.
from: Brilliant's Scientific Thinking course (brilliant.org/courses/puzzle-science: levels Gears, Mobiles, Pool, Structures, Optics, Compound Gears; puzzles with no number-crunching), and its Physics of the Everyday and Classical Mechanics courses for the same ground with numbers
others: the AQA GCSE Physics (8463) and Combined Science specifications (moments, levers and gears; momentum; forces in equilibrium; reflection and refraction), BBC Bitesize GCSE physics pages on the same, OpenStax College Physics (statics, momentum and collisions, geometric optics), and Isaac Physics where it has these puzzles
syllabi: Dan's January course (a one-week Leading Rate marine engineering enabling course that tests maths and physics at GCSE level in relation to engineering; its syllabus is not public, so plan against GCSE physics and say where a choice is a guess): the GCSE physics subject content (DfE) and its list of equations to recall (moments, momentum, weight, refractive index where present), AQA 8463's required content lines on moments, levers and gears, momentum, and reflection and refraction, and the public apprenticeship standard lines for a maritime mechanical fitter or naval engineering technician that need moments, gear trains, momentum, structures or optics. Exact lines
scope: Dan asked (2 Nov) for visual and interactive puzzles with some mathematics, following Brilliant's Scientific Thinking but adding the working Brilliant leaves out. Seven lessons in this order: (1) Gears: meshing gears turn opposite ways, an idler keeps direction, an odd loop jams; speed times teeth is the same on both gears (n1 T1 = n2 T2). (2) Compound gear trains: two gears on one shaft turn together; the train ratio is the stage ratios multiplied; the fastest gear; speed traded for torque with power the same. (3) Balancing mobiles: moments about a pivot, clockwise equals anticlockwise, adding moments, levels hung from levels, a mystery weight, then two unknowns solved together. (4) Collisions (pool): momentum before equals momentum after, chain reactions, glancing hits split into components, elastic or not (kinetic energy kept or lost). (5) Structures: why a triangle is rigid and a square is not (degrees of freedom), support reactions on a beam by moments, tension or compression in each bar by balancing forces at a joint, a screw as a ramp. (6) Mirrors: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, aiming mirrors, where an image sits and its apparent distance, two mirrors in a periscope (general physics only). (7) Refraction and prisms: light bending at a boundary, refractive index n = c/v, things in water looking shallower, Snell's law with trigonometry, the critical angle and total internal reflection in a prism, dispersion into colours. Each lesson opens with a puzzle he can feel his way through, then the rule, then typed-answer puzzles he works on paper, GCSE-exam style (equations recalled, units given). He has Mechanics and materials (moments, gears, momentum, statics) and the maths courses (Trigonometry, Vectors, Linear systems): lessons 1 to 5 build on them as puzzles and practice, never a re-teach of the rule from scratch; lessons 6 and 7 are new ground. Examples from gearboxes, winches, cranes and lifting beams, and a periscope where they fit; never claim how the Navy or a boat does it
later: Circuits (same folder: current, voltage and resistance as puzzles)
Waves and light (Physics folder: waves, sound and the wave equation; this course takes only reflection and refraction)
